#3516. 12 Perfect Christmas Movies Nobody Talks About

Halloween is over, so according to the gods of commerce, it's officially Christmas season. That means many of us will soon begin our seasonal movie watching, returning to a wide variety of X-mas classics that span from It's a Wonderful Life to Die Hard. There are a lot of Christmas movies that are perfect for this time of year, offering moods that make us feel everything from warm and fuzzy to dark and depressed. Beyond all those classics, though, there are a number of equally perfect Christmas movies that haven't dominated the conversation enough.

These lesser-discussed Christmas movies cover the Yuletide spectrum from naughty to nice, full of sugary delights and some harsh spices as well. There are new animated masterpieces, classic Westerns, and neo-noir thrillers. There's something under the tree for any kind of Christmas movie fan, whether you're an optimistic Buddy the Elf or a cynical Grinch. We're making a list, checking it twice, and we're gonna find out what perfect Christmas movies no one is talking about.

The Western genre doesn't exactly lend itself to heartwarming tales of Christmas. The dusty locations don't inspire Yuletide cheer, and even those that are set in snowy locations are more frigid and cold-blooded than festive and warmhearted. That didn't stop John Ford and John Wayne from using the Christmas season for their biblically inspired Western 3 Godfathers. Based on the short story The Three Godfathers by Peter B. Kyne, which had been adapted to film several times before, the movie offers a retelling of the fable of the Three Wise Men that swaps the New Testament for the Old West.

Bob (Wayne), Pete (Pedro Armendariz), and the Abilene Kid (Harry Carey Jr.) are three outlaws who rob a bank and go on the run into the desert. Their escape plans are complicated when they come across a dying woman who gives birth to a child and makes them promise to take care of the baby. A more sentimental Western than fans might expect from the collaboration of Ford and Wayne, 3 Godfathers offers some perfect Holiday counterprogramming for genre fans.

If you need more trios of criminals at Christmastime, then We're No Angels is the perfect stocking stuffer. Based on a Broadway play adapted from a French original, the film was the final collaboration between director Michael Curtiz and Humphrey Bogart, but it hasn't enjoyed the same legacy as their biggest movie together. Co-starring Peter Ustinov and Aldo Ray, it's a darkly comical Christmas movie that taps into the seasonal themes of redemption and goodwill.

Joseph (Bogart), Albert (Ray), and Jules (Ustinov) are three convicts who have escaped from Devil's Island at Christmastime, ending up in a colonial town in French Guiana where they ingratiate themselves with the locals to aid their getaway plans. Over time, the trio comes to care for the residents, who soften their hardened criminal hearts. We're No Angels is the perfect mix of breezy comedy and crime movie elements, with the three leads giving criminally overlooked performances.

Criminals make for seemingly perfect Christmas movie protagonists, as evidenced by the prior two films on this list. Blast of Silence continues that trend but with a far more cynical tone befitting a film noir. Directed by and starring Allen Baron, the film was shot on a low budget in New York City, lending it a gritty authenticity that also makes it a black-and-white Christmas card for the city during the time period. It's a lean, mean little thriller that makes perfect use of the juxtaposition between the bright holiday lights and the dark shadows.

Frankie (Baron) is a mob hitman who has come home for the holidays to carry out a contract. While he bides his time plotting and planning the hit, Frankie also meets up with friends from his past, which brings up all kinds of demons within him. Not all Christmas movies are designed to be uplifting experiences, and Blast of Silence is one of the best at making you feel bad. It's a dark neo-noir thriller that's a great gift for the Christmas cynic in your family.

There have been so many adaptations of Charles Dickens' seminal A Christmas Carol that some were naturally going to be forgotten along the way. Everyone has their personal favorite cinematic interpretation of the tale of Ebenezer Scrooge, from the 1951 classic starring Alistair Sim to George C. Scott's more abrasive take on the character. One that should be at the top of everyone's Christmas list is the Academy Award-winning animated short film directed by Richard Williams. Both Sim and actor Michael Hordern reprise their roles as Scrooge and Marley, respectively, and the film is a properly haunting adaptation.

Running only 25 minutes, the short film manages to hit all the highlights from the Dickens novel, and even includes a few moments often left out of other adaptations. The hand-drawn animation lends itself to the material, evoking 19th-century illustrations and giving the ghost story a proper element of darkness and danger. Williams, who's probably best known as the animation director on Who Framed Roger Rabbit, is a true legend of animation, and his rendition of the quintessential Christmas story should be more renowned.

Every one of these four started as a cast recording people played until the disc wore out, and every one of them eventually turned into a film. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You work like the clock is against you, because in your head it always is. Hamilton is three hours about a man who cannot stop producing, cannot stop arguing and cannot leave a single thing alone, and you recognised yourself in it immediately.

People made up their minds about you early and they were wrong. Wicked takes the most famous villain in American children's fiction and asks what the story looks like from her side, which is a question you have asked about yourself more than once.

You cannot walk past something unfair. Les Mis is a show about a man who spends his entire life trying to make one wrong right, and about everybody around him deciding what they are prepared to lose for other people.

You are not interested in saving it all for later. Rent is a year in the life of people with no money, no plan and a very clear sense that the time they have is the only thing they genuinely own.

One of the most popular adaptations of A Christmas Carol happens to be the one starring a felt frog and a pig. The Muppet Christmas Carol has become a perennial favorite for many, but it's not the first time Jim Henson's beloved characters have tackled the holiday. A Muppet Family Christmas was a television special that featured not only the titular characters, but also members from Sesame Street and Fraggle Rock as well. It's an absolutely charming movie musical which has also unfortunately fallen by the wayside due to its unavailability on streaming and the fact that most physical media releases have had to cut some songs due to rights issues.

The special follows the entire Muppets cast as they head to Fozzie Bear's mom's house for Christmas, turning it into an absolute madhouse. The Swedish Chef tries to cook Big Bird for Christmas dinner, Fozzie tries to form a double act with a talking snowman, and everyone forgets to mind the icy patch in front of the door. A Muppet Family Christmas has everything to satisfy fans of the Muppets and more. It's a sweet, funny, perfect Christmas special.

See if you can guess the Christmas movie from this premise: A young boy is left alone at home during the holiday season and has to defend himself against a home invader through the use of booby traps. If you answered Home Alone, you'd be correct. You'd also be correct if you answered 3615 Père Noël, also known as Deadly Games and Dial Code Santa Claus, the French horror-action-comedy which many have compared to the Macaulay Culkin classic, including director René Manzor, who unsuccessfully tried to pursue legal action against the producers.

There's never been any official confirmation that Home Alone was ripped off from Manzor's film, and the differences in tone and style become quickly apparent when watching them. Thomas (Alain Lalanne) is similarly resourceful as Kevin McCallister, but he's more inspired by Rambo and other action heroes, which serves him well after an attempted phone call to Santa Claus attracts the attention of a deranged man who breaks into Thomas' high-tech home while his mom is at work. As an homage to '80s action movies, 3615 Père Noël brings on the set pieces and violence, but also a surprising amount of holiday spirit. It makes for the perfect Christmas double feature with Home Alone.

Here's another holiday home invasion. This one comes in the form of an acerbic burglar who takes a WASPy couple hostage while on the run from the police. The Ref comes from director Ted Demme and received solid reviews when it was released but was a box office disappointment. It's since gained a minor cult following, but remains far less celebrated in comparison to other Christmas dark comedies. Its only real sin is having Kevin Spacey in its cast, but at the time it was made, that was actually considered a good idea.

Gus (Denis Leary) is a thief on a job in a wealthy neighborhood that goes south, so he takes a rich couple, Lloyd (Spacey) and Caroline (Judy Davis), hostage and forces them to harbor him in their home. Gus doesn't get the silent night he's hoping for since Lloyd and Caroline are having marital issues, and the thief unwittingly serves as counselor between the two of them. The Ref is sharply written and acted, and was a precursor to darker Christmas comedies like Bad Santa.

Inspired by the aforementioned 3 Godfathers, Tokyo Godfathers is an animated masterpiece from acclaimed director Satoshi Kon. It similarly follows three lost souls who find themselves taking care of an infant on Christmas Eve, but this version of the story takes some unexpected detours and finds shining moments of humanity amid its dark odyssey into the night. Gorgeously animated and determinedly unconventional, Tokyo Godfathers is the perfect Christmas movie for those who are sick of the same old holiday lessons.

In Tokyo, the homeless Gin, Hana, and Miyuki find an abandoned baby along with items to help them track down the child's parents. Their adventure takes them across the city and into contact with all sorts of colorful figures. Tokyo Godfathers is less surreal than Kon's other masterworks, Perfect Blue, Millennium Actress, and Paprika, but is no less creative. Its miracles are all the work of real people rather than any magical beings, and the film itself finds magic in found families and the triumph of the human spirit.

If there's any screenwriter most associated with Christmas, it's Shane Black. The writer has infused the holiday into most of his screenplays and films, from Lethal Weapon to Iron Man 3, but none more perfectly than his neo-noir directorial debut Kiss Kiss Bang Bang. As a two-hander between Robert Downey Jr. and Val Kilmer, the film is filled with all the witty banter Black is best known for and similarly offers a pulpy mystery set in the City of Angels during the most wonderful time of the year.

Harry Lockhart (Downey) is a thief who makes his way from New York to Los Angeles by posing as an aspiring actor. While attending parties in the Hollywood Hills and wooing his hometown crush, Harry also gets involved in a murder mystery, causing him to join forces with private investigator Perry van Shrike (Kilmer). Kiss Kiss Bang Bang wasn't the same kind of blockbuster success as the films Black wrote in the '80s and '90s, but it's a perfect gift for fans of his.

Despite the presence of several animated films on this list, none of them feature stop-motion animation, the medium most associated with Christmas thanks to specials like Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. While there are some underrated stop-motion Christmas movies worth checking out, they can't quite match the perfection of Arthur Christmas, a computer-animated film from Aardman. That studio built itself on stop-motion with characters like Wallace and Gromit, but their first Christmas movie has all the same charm despite being wholly digital.

Arthur (James McAvoy) is the youngest son of Santa (Jim Broadbent). He's clumsy, awkward, and far from the tech-savvy professional his brother Steve (Hugh Laurie) is, but he does have plenty of Christmas spirit. So, when a child is missed on Christmas Eve, Arthur takes it upon himself to get the present delivered, with the help of his elderly Grandsanta (Bill Nighy). Filled with wildly inventive set pieces and indelible characters, Arthur Christmas offers a unique take on the Santa Claus mythos, and it delivers it with a perfect earnestness.

#3515. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

WhatsApp is rolling out an update to Events just in time for holiday get-togethers. Guests can open an invite link, see the event details, and RSVP without creating a WhatsApp account or downloading the app.

I run every day and while I prefer to do those runs outside, having access to a treadmill can be a lifesaver at times.

The Urevo CyberMega came in clutch during my recent training block for the Frankfurt Marathon, and it impressed me during workouts with its high top speed and connectivity, and then was easy to store afterwards thanks to the fact it folds fully flat.

I rated it highly at its full price of $999 in my four-star review, and right now you can get the Urevo CyberMega for $899 in the early Black Friday sales.

The Urevo CyberMega offers impressive specs at a lower price than most treadmills, and it's fold-flat design makes it easy to store as well. It's $100 off right now in the Amazon sale, which is the cheapest I've ever seen it.

It’s not a huge discount, but $899 is an outstanding price for such a capable machine. It has a top speed of 12.5mph and a max incline of 12%, and you can link it directly to both the Urevo app and third-party options like Zwift to follow scenic routes and guided workouts on a tablet.

The space-saving design is a double-edged sword, in that the Urevo CyberMega has a fairly small running belt. I’m 6ft and found it OK to use even at the machine’s highest speeds, but don’t expect the spacious feel you get on gym-standard treadmills.

The big advantage of the smaller design is storage though. I’ve used huge treadmills from the likes of Bowflex and Peloton in the past, and having now tried the smaller, foldable CyberMega, I wouldn’t go back to a really big machine.

Not only is it easy to store flat under something or secured against a wall, the CyberMega is also easier to move around, which is important to me as I mostly use it in the garage but need to bring it inside sometimes to run while my kids are asleep.

I can’t yet speak to the durability of the machine having only tested it for a couple of months, but so far it looks a great value option for runners who need a foldable machine with a high top speed, and getting an extra $100 off only sweetens the deal.

#3512. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3510. All 3 ‘NCIS’ Shows Officially Return to CBS Tonight

Although the entire NCIS franchise has been on a roll to start the fall television season, the trio of crime procedurals ran into the one thing that could stop them last week — democracy. Midterm coverage meant Parker, Gibbs, Hanna, and the rest took the night off while the results of House, Senate, and other elections rolled in. It's far from unusual for network programs to be preempted at some point in the fall, especially for those airing on Tuesday nights in an even year, but it nonetheless slowed the series' momentum at a time when the franchise ratings are at a high. Fortunately for fans, their absence on CBS won't last any longer.

All three of NCIS, NCIS: New York, and NCIS: Origins are locked in to return tonight in their usual time slots, starting with the flagship at 8 p.m. ET/PT. Season 24 has been riding a ratings high with the reintroduction of Michael Weatherly's fan-favorite agent Tony DiNozzo as the new director of NCIS in place of the late Leon Vance (Rocky Carroll). As part of a strong CBS premiere week, the series returned with a 20% increase in viewers over the previous season's first episode, drawing in 6.45 million viewers and carrying the momentum in Nielsen's live plus 7 days of multiplatform viewership. Episode 5, "Speechless," will next send the team to take on the case of an eight-year-old girl, played by NCIS star Katrina Law's own daughter, Kinley Andreen, left alone when her Marine mother goes missing. In a race against time to find her parent, they learn the lengths the mom was willing to go to for her family and discover that their shy witness' unexpected skill may be the key to blowing their search open.

The newcomer New York, meanwhile, will continue Sam Hanna's (LL COOL J) homecoming at 9 p.m., with an episode that hits close to home for his new partner, Nick Schaeffer (Scott Caan). The Big Apple's agents are called in to investigate after a naval interrogator is violently murdered in her own home. In the background, however, the corruption investigation into Nick's old partner is still unfolding, and he's unsure how to process it all. Finally, at 10 p.m., Origins will continue where its previous episode left off with "Baila Esta Cumbia," as Gibbs (Mark Harmon) and Bishop (Emily Wickersham) continue their off-the-books mission with an intense interrogation while, in 1993, Franks (Kyle Schmid) leads the team on a murder case involving a con woman that hits Lala (Mariel Molino) especially hard.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

While Weatherly's return as Tony and Harmon's return as Gibbs have both drawn extra attention to NCIS and Origins early on, at least one of them will be gone from the screen once more before the year ends. With the addition of the LL-led New York to the lineup, Origins is one of several series CBS cut down to just ten episodes instead of the 18 its past two runs have clocked in at. The shortened Season 3 means the finale is expected to air in December, leaving room for NCIS: Sydney to return for Season 4 sometime next year. That means only five episodes are left after tonight to wrap up one of the most dangerous and personal cases of Gibbs' career that has tied so deeply into his past at Camp Pendleton.

NCIS, NCIS: New York, and NCIS: Origins air tonight on CBS. Stay tuned here at Collider for more changes in scheduled programming throughout the rest of the year.

#3508. Six Fitness 'Rules' That Don't Actually Matter

I’ve learned a lot in my many years in the gym, and beginner-me would be shocked and appalled by the things present-me does during workouts. With the benefit of experience, I now do exercises I used to think one should “never” do, and I’ve broken pretty much every other rule besides.

I've already explained a bunch of things you can stop worrying about as a beginner, but I’d like to expand on that list with a few more rules that even intermediate-level exercisers can ditch without consequence.

If you can theoretically do 13 bicep curls with a certain weight, how many curls should you actually do? One common misconception is that if you don’t do all 13, you’re leaving gains on the table. The rule kind of makes sense if you have truly no clue where to start; if you go until you can’t do a single rep more, then at least you know you’re not slacking off.

But the downside is that going to failure for every set of every lift is just going to make you exhausted. On bicep curls, maybe not so much, but once you’re squatting pretty heavy weights, you’re going to feel spent if you do every single set to failure, and that fatigue will get in the way of getting a good workout in consistently. What’s better is to follow a program that advises you on when to hold back and when it’s a good time to really push your limits. You’ll find that most of the time, you stop a set at least 2-3 reps shy of failure, and sometimes even more.

Rest days are a convenient tool for making sure you’re not overworking yourself, but that’s all. Organizations like the American College of Sports Medicine recommend leaving 48 hours between intense strength-training sessions for a given muscle, but if you look at where they get that number, it’s meant to be a general recommendation for beginners and for people who are exercising just to stay healthy. Once you’re talking about athletes or enthusiasts, the ACSM acknowledges that training most days of the week is fine if your program manages fatigue effectively. That may mean alternating between heavier and lighter days, rather than taking complete rest days.

The “10% rule” is a not-terrible guideline for figuring out how quickly to ramp up your training. But like many of these other myths, it’s a suggestion, not a commandment to be strictly obeyed.

As running coach Jason Fitzgerald told Lifehacker, “While the adage is to only increase weekly mileage by 10%, this may be either too conservative or even too aggressive depending on where you start from.” When you’re coming back from a short layoff, you can probably increase mileage a lot faster. Same goes if you’re a beginner and your mileage is overall very low; if you took the rule literally, you wouldn’t be able to increase from zero to any other number.

Meanwhile, serious running programs—once again, a program is a wonderful thing—may give you a bigger increase for a few weeks in a row, then cut back and decrease your mileage temporarily before ramping up again. Or they may keep you at the same mileage for weeks at a time before venturing a larger increase. If you were to stick to the 10% rule, you would miss out on the advantages of programs that work this way.

There are pros and cons to lifting before cardio, and to doing cardio before lifting. It’s more of an “it depends” than a rule. So here are some of the ways to decide which makes sense.

Your lifts tend to suffer when you’re fatigued, and doing them fresh is important to you

Cardio is your top priority, and you want to have more energy for it

Your lifts are the kind of thing that can get done even when you’re fatigued

Or you only intend to do a small amount of cardio before lifting

So a cyclist may prefer to do a strength workout after hopping off the bike, but a powerlifter would probably rather get their conditioning in after finishing squats for the day. Either is fine if you don’t care, or if you prefer to mix it up.

There are a few supplements that can help you in your fitness journey, but none of them are necessary. Creatine is one of the best-known muscle-building supplements. It’s understood to be effective, but here’s the thing: Just because it does something for most people doesn’t mean it does very much. If you decide it’s too expensive or just that you would rather not have another thing to remember to take every day, you’re not missing out on any substantial amount of gains.

Likewise, protein powder is a helpful way to get more protein in your diet, but you don’t need to use a supplement; you can just eat more protein-containing foods.

And finally, pre-workout drinks can give you more energy in the gym (it’s mostly caffeine), but the idea that you need it is a very recent development. Even ten years ago, it wasn’t really a thing. People showed up to the gym with a coffee or a coke or with no caffeine at all in their stomach, and worked out just fine.

Look, people have been exercising successfully for millennia, but all of our apps and devices weren't even a thing until the 2000s. Tracking every minute, every step, or every mile of your routine is not actually necessary. You’re still a runner even if you don’t have an app that knows how many miles you ran. You don’t even have to track your sets and reps in your lifting journal if you don’t want to. Your body is what knows how much work you put in, even if your phone were to get wiped overnight.

Amazon has cut the price of its latest Fire TV Stick 4K, dropping it to $24.99 from $59.99 and bringing it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, it's an affordable way to bring 4K streaming to an older television or give a sluggish smart TV a performance upgrade. And because this streaming stick measures just 3.6 inches and draws power directly from your TV's USB port using the included cable, it can sit out of sight behind your screen without taking up another wall outlet.

What you don't get is Dolby Vision or Dolby Atmos audio. If either is important to your home theater setup, the Fire TV Stick 4K Plus, currently $39.99, is worth considering for the extra $15. Otherwise, there's little to complain about when it comes to performance, with PCMag reporting that apps respond almost instantly and 4K streams load quickly with almost no blurry, low-resolution moments.

The redesigned Alexa voice remote is another improvement, with a more comfortable shape, an easier-to-find home button, and dedicated shortcuts for major streaming services. The software experience is less impressive, with advertisements and recommendations dominating the home screen, leaving relatively little room for your actual apps. There's also no support for Apple AirPlay or Google Cast, so sharing content directly from your phone isn't particularly convenient. #3503. iOS 27.3 gives Apple One’s high-end tier a compelling upgrade

iOS 27.3 is coming next month and is packed with new features, including some that make Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Apple One launched in 2019 with Individual, Family, and Premier plans. And in the seven years since, the service bundle has stayed remarkably consistent.

Every plan has always included Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, and iCloud+. And the high-end Premier option adds Apple News+ and Fitness+ alongside more iCloud storage.

Apple News+ has gotten a lot better over the years. Following the New York Times playbook, Apple has added daily puzzle games, food-focused content like recipes, and audio stories, all while continuing to improve the basic news experience.

Apple Fitness+ keeps improving too, but there’s an upgrade in iOS 27.3 that makes it far more compelling in my view: Gym Strength.

Built-in video demonstrations accompany your personalized plan, making strength training accessible even for newcomers. And you can track your progress in the app, with key Apple Watch integration too.

I’ve used Fitness+ plenty and enjoyed it, but a comprehensive strength plan like this was a big gap in the service previously. With iOS 27.3 though, Fitness+ takes a big leap forward and makes Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Also relevant: with the new HomeView product and other Apple Home accessories almost here, Apple One Premier’s support for Apple Intelligence video summaries and clips with HomeKit Secure Video becomes more valuable. All of this together amounts to a stronger-than-ever Premier plan.

Apple One starts at $21.95/month and includes services like Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+, and more.

#3501. 5 Best Death-Game Books for ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ Fans, Ranked

Millions of readers have now taken a chance on Dungeon Crawler Carl, though many online profess that they've never read a "LitRPG" story before. The obscure subgenre is an odd quirk for many fans, with some diving into other titles and many wondering if they'll really like anything beyond DCC. However, on a simpler level Dungeon Crawler Carl sticks to a familiar format in the sci-fi/fantasy genre: the "death game." Stories about deadly competitions have been popular in speculative fiction for years, from tournaments and tests of strength to bloody trials and rites of passage. There's nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, but the books below are a great starting point for DCC fans looking for their next binge.

The LitRPG setting is brilliant for death game fiction because it allows the author to flesh out all the rules and mechanics in extreme detail. It becomes more than worldbuilding minutiae when the characters' lives depend on these rules, and Dungeon Crawler Carl has a lot of fun playing with the absurdity of it all. Still, many fans are weary of exploring more LitRPG without the overwhelming recommendations DCC already has behind it. For those that want another death game after DCC without with the LitRPG format, here are five books you might enjoy.

If you've picked up Dungeon Crawler Carl within the last year or two, chances are you did so knowing about it's meteoric rise in popularity. As long as you're catching up on popular ongoing series, you might as well give the works of Sarah J. Maas a try. Today, the author is best known for her series A Court of Thorns and Roses, but prior to that she wrote an eight-book series called Throne of Glass. The two series are loosely connected as they take place in the same universe — though in different dimensions.

Throne of Glass follows a young assassin named Celaena Sardothien, who is imprisoned and on the verge of death when the series begins. Celaena's only chance at freedom is competing in a series of contests to choose the "King's Champion." She goes up against other assassins and warriors in a series of extremely dangerous competitions before finally facing the survivors in one-on-one duels. As if that wasn't dangerous enough, someone is picking off the contestants one by one behind the scenes, apparently in an attempt to affect the outcome of the games.

Sticking with topical picks, Stephen King's 1982 novel The Running Man is about a death game that comes pretty close to Dungeon Crawler Carl in terms of bleak absurdity. The book is set in a near future where economic collapse has left many Americans in desperate poverty. In the midst of this, a reality show called The Running Man seems to offer a way out — but at great risk. Contestants must avoid teams of hitmen sent out by the producers to kill them. They win money based on how long they stay alive, but viewers can also win money by turning them in, making things incredibly difficult. When the story begins, no contestant has ever survived to win the grand prize, but their families do get $100 for every hour they managed to stay alive.

The Running Man was adapted into a film in 1987 starring Arnold Schwarzenegger, though it diverged wildly from King's novel. Another adaptation was released just last year. It starred Glen Powell and stuck much more closely to the story. Fans will have three versions of the story to contrast and compare, and each one evokes the same kind of righteous fury as Dungeon Crawler Carl.

Of course, The Hunger Games series is one of the most iconic death game stories in recent decades, and it deserves a place on this list. For those that have watched the movies but not read the books, there are some very interesting differences to explore on the page. On top of that, Suzanne Collins' more recent prequel novels are even more interesting as they step outside of Katniss' first-person perspective and reveal more of Collins' range as an author.

The Hunger Games is also set in a dystopian near-future U.S.A. which is in the grip of a ruthless totalitarian regime. After several attempts at revolution, the ruling class instituted an annual spectacle called The Hunger Games in which two teenagers from every district are sent as "tribute" to compete in a battle royale competition. The books keep their focus on these death games throughout the story, though they do veer into plenty of other interesting territory along the way.

Many fans of Dungeon Crawler Carl are reaching for Pierce Brown's Red Rising series as well, and the death game aspect is just one more reason to recommend it. The novels introduce us to a distant future where humanity has thoroughly colonized the entire solar system, yet most people live under the yoke of a brutal caste system which is maintained with genetic engineering, social engineering, and brute force. The story follows a young man named Darrow who is secretly elevated from the lowest caste — red — to the highest — gold — to try and sabotage the rulers from within.

Darrow then participates in a ritualistic death game in order to join the elite ranks of ruling golds where he may be able to affect the most change. He and dozens of other teenage candidates must survive for months in a brutally sculpted wilderness, warring with each other to survive and dominate. It's not the focus of the entire series, but it's a brilliant introduction to Brown's sci-fi setting which sticks with you throughout the remaining books. Red Rising is nearly finished now, with Brown working on the final volume as we speak. It has also been greenlit for a film adaptation, so now is a great time to get onboard.

Finally, The Poppy War trilogy by R.F. Kuang is a must-read for modern fantasy fans, including DCC fans. Like Red Rising, its death game element is just one chapter among many, but it stands out and defines the characters in all the fights that follow. The Poppy War is set in a fantasy world inspired by China and other East Asian cultures. Protagonist Rin makes it into the Nikara Empire military academy despite her impoverished background, and is determined to rise through the ranks at any cost. She is drawn to the obscure field of shamanism, using meditation and psychoactive drugs to harness magical powers. Through her work, her perspective on the empire begins to shift.

The Poppy War is often billed as "grimdark." Dungeon Crawler Carl fans may think they're prepared for that, but there is little levity or absurdity to balance out the heartbreak here. Still, this is one of the best fantasy trilogies to come out in the last decade, and it has launched Kuang into a stellar career. It should be at the top of the TBR for fantasy fans with a book hangover.

All the books mentioned above are available now in print, digital, and audiobook formats, as is Dungeon Crawler Carl. The DCC TV adaptation is in production now, and the ninth book is well underway. So far, neither has a release date.

Amazon has knocked $100 off the latest Google Pixel Watch 5 (45mm, LTE), bringing it down to $429.99 from $529.99, its lowest price yet, according to price trackers. If you can do without cellular connectivity, the 45mm wifi model is also down by $100, now selling for a record-low $329.99 (down from $429.99). Plus, either one comes with 90 days of free Amazon Music. PCMag calls the Pixel Watch 5 the best smartwatch for Android users, largely because Gemini is built in so deeply—the assistant works proactively, so it can surface your flight details on the way to the airport or suggest a contact's number while you text about dinner plans, and a new AI-powered Health Coach reviews your workouts with tailored feedback, though some of its fitness advice sits behind a paid subscription.

Helping all of those AI features along is a faster Qualcomm processor that Google says improves the overall performance of this smartwatch by 20%, while RAM increases from 2GB to 3GB and storage doubles to 64GB compared with the Pixel Watch 4. The iPhone Duo launch has not been without its problems, and I don't mean the lengthy waits people are suffering to get hold of one. Some users are experiencing what has been dubbed "crackgate," with their internal screens breaking for seemingly no reason. Nobody is quite sure what the problem is, but one leaker claims Apple may have figured out which phones could be affected.

According to Kang on Weibo (via Ice Universe), the issue itself has been traced to "defective materials" at one of Apple's two hinge suppliers. They claim this isn't an issue with the hinge design, which presumably explains why it hasn't affected more Duo users.

Then again, it's impossible to tell how many Duo users are out there, considering how limited the initial supply seems to be. Plus, social media posts give a very distorted view of just how many screens have broken, and all we have from Apple is a claim that "only a small number of iPhone Duo units" are affected.

Kang says Apple can identify the affected iPhone Duos from their serial numbers, which should mean the company can be more proactive in how it deals with the crackgate problem. However, it's unclear what Apple's plans are and how it intends to deal with this botched batch of Duo units.

One suggested solution is to give users the ability to check their serial numbers with a tool, which will check and see if they received one of the tainted hinges. Alternatively Apple could just sit and wait for the screens to break, and organize repairs or replacements for the affected customers.

Obviously the former would be a better option, assuming Apple can't reach out to them directly, and it would put a stop to the images of broken iPhone Duos being posted on social media.

Hopefully, if Apple has identified the problematic hinges, it should mean that the problem will eventually go away by itself. Though it remains to be seen whether this will affect how long people will be waiting for their own iPhone Duo deliveries, since we have no idea how many units have been produced with the substandard hinges.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

But hey, if this leak is on the money, then Apple hasn't screwed up the design of the iPhone Duo, and turned its first foldable into an inevitable time bomb. Any of you still waiting for your Duo to arrive should end up with a working unit. As for anyone who already has the Apple foldable, it's unclear what might happen.

Word on social media is that you will see a raised bump on the hinge in the run-up to the screen breaking. If you see that, or anything else out of the ordinary, be sure to get in touch with Apple. Or head to your nearest Apple Store if you can.

Apple has said that it is bypassing standard repair wait times and offering free device replacements under the standard manufacturing warranty for Duo users with cracked screens. What's more, affected users don't need to have a paid AppleCare+ plan to get a replacement for this specific problem.

#3496. tvOS 27.2 adds new Apple TV 4K setting that’s an instant favorite

tvOS 27.2 launched last week as the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it includes a new setting I’m a big fan of: Shuffle for screen savers.

Screen savers have been one of the best Apple TV features since tvOS first launched in 2015. Largely that’s due to the gorgeous aerials captured around the world (and even from space).

Aerials are still my favorite type of Apple TV screen saver, but tvOS has steadily added other categories worth checking out too.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

The second and third options tap into your Apple Photos library and introduce the joy of seeing your favorite memories pop up on the big screen. Snoopy screen savers feature the beloved Peanuts character in a variety of entertaining scenes.

All of these screen saver options are great. But until tvOS 27.2, you had to select just one category and that’s all you’d ever see.

Now with tvOS 27.2, Apple has introduced a ‘Shuffle’ option that randomly cycles through screen savers from across all four categories.

It’s a welcome new setting, long overdue but I’ve been enjoying it a lot. The ability to be surprised by more different screen savers may sound like a small thing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to the Apple TV 4K experience.

Have you tried the new Shuffle setting for screen savers in tvOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3495. Original Harry Potter Star Officially Confirms Franchise Return Ahead of HBO Series

The release of HBO's Harry Potter is just a few weeks away at this point, and it feels like the entire world is watching and waiting to rejoin the Wizarding World. However, there are a select few who have already been there, and when given the opportunity to head back to Hogwarts, it seems like they just couldn't say no.

Speaking exclusively with Collider's Steve Weintraub while promoting his upcoming movie Ebenezer, Rupert Grint revealed that his return as Ron Weasley in Broadway's Harry Potter and the Cursed Child will probably be the last time he plays the character. The actor is scheduled to begin his limited engagement at New York's Lyric Theatre on February 2, 2027. Grint explained that, after just over 15 years away from the role, it felt like the right time because, not only does he now have a family of his own, but he's also reached roughly the same age as Ron in the stage production. Grint told Collider:

"It's funny, kind of, it's interesting. Kind of going back, I think I spent so much time after finishing Potter moving away from it and doing other things which I really enjoy doing. But I think now it's a very different Ron in a very different context, and weirdly, it's lined up that I'm kind of the exact age of the character in that story. So it just felt like a good time, and I love New York and being on stage. It's been a while since I've done that, and it's a very important thing to me. It was my childhood, and I have a very strong connection to that character and that world. And I think I'm not going to get many other opportunities to play him again. It probably is my last, and I think it'll be fun."

Grint previously made his Broadway debut in It's Only a Play in 2014, but returning to the stage as a character he's known for most of his life presents an entirely different challenge, and he admitted that he couldn't resist the challenge, while confessing the nostalgia had been a delight. "Well, yeah. I mean, it's very nostalgic," said Grint. "Even for me, it's fun to kind of go back and get back into that world. It's been a while." Of course, Weintraub couldn't resist asking the question that just about every Harry Potter fan will be thinking: could Grint persuade Radcliffe and Watson to join him on Broadway for a reunion?

"It would be fun. I don't know. I mean, it's obviously different for everyone. It was an intense kind of time. When we finished, I really enjoyed stepping away and not really even thinking about it. Because it was such an intense... I mean, it was enjoyable, and they looked after us. But it was a big part of us. So yeah, maybe. I don't know. It'd be fun."

Before Grint returns to Hogwarts, audiences will get to see him in Ebenezer, a new adaptation of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol starring Johnny Depp (Pirates of the Caribbean) as Ebenezer Scrooge, and directed by Ti West. Grint plays Bob Cratchit, the father of Tiny Tim. The tale has been adapted many times for the screen. It's a thrilling ghost story set in Dickens’ London that follows one man’s supernatural journey to face his past, present, and future — and his fight for a second chance.

In addition to Grint, the film stars Andrea Riseborough (To Leslie) as the Ghost of Christmas Past, Sam Claflin (The Hunger Games) as Fred, Daisy Ridley (Star Wars: The Force Awakens) as Clara, Arthur Conti (Beetlejuice Beetlejuice) as Young Ebenezer, Ellie Bamber (Willow) as Belle, Tramell Tillman (Severance) as the Ghost of Christmas Present, and Ian McKellen (The Lord of the Rings) as Jacob Marley. The screenplay comes from Nathaniel Halpern, with Emma Watts producing. Ebenezer opens in theaters on November 13, 2026.

Rupert Grint begins his limited Broadway engagement as Ron Weasley in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child on February 2, 2027, with performances scheduled through May 30. #3494. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

“Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself,” Anthropic says. “With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Similar to ChatGPT’s finances feature, Claude’s new capabilities essentially give you a way to use chat as a way to make sense of your finance data. It can also present data in dashboards, calendars, and more.

Given the importance of security, here’s what Anthropic has to say regarding the new finance feature and Claude:

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That’s where you agree to its terms and approve Claude’s read-only access, so Claude doesn’t ask for or see your bank password.

Microsoft’s flagship development tool, Visual Studio Professional 2026, reduces much of the friction that used to come with large projects, and it’s on sale for just $29.97 on StackSocial right now, which is far less than what most developers expect to pay for a professional-grade IDE.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. Visual Studio 2026 supports C#, C++, .NET, ASP.NET, Blazor, and .NET MAUI, so you can move between desktop, web, and cross-platform projects without switching tools. You also get Hot Reload, which helps reduce rebuild time by letting you edit code in .NET and C++ apps and see changes immediately. And CodeLens adds useful context right inside the editor—who last edited a method, which tests cover it, and whether recent changes broke anything—without forcing you to dig through menus or version history. The software’s AI-powered IntelliCode suggestions also feel more restrained than flashy. They tend to fill in logical patterns based on your existing code. It saves time on repetitive work, but you’ll still want to read what it writes.

Collaboration is another area where this version earns its keep. Live Share allows teammates to jump into a debugging or editing session without cloning the repo or matching environments. That’s useful for code reviews or troubleshooting, but it depends heavily on a stable internet connection. System requirements are also worth noting: While it can technically run on 4GB of RAM, 8GB or more is far more realistic, especially for larger solutions, and storage needs can balloon depending on workloads, reaching well over 100GB in some setups. Also, it doesn’t support 32-bit systems and won’t run on mobile devices or Chromebooks. For developers already working in the Windows ecosystem, this is a solid long-term license. For everyone else, those limitations can be deal breakers.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a full-featured, 64-bit IDE for Windows designed for developers working on complex, multi-project codebases, and it's on sale right now for a one-time price of $29.97 on StackSocial.

#3487. ABC Is Failing ‘High Potential’ and ‘The Rookie’ Once Again

ABC's fall procedural lineup has just two weeks left until it airs its mid-season finales and goes on hiatus for the winter, but the premiere dates for the spring lineup have only just been announced. Like 9-1-1, 9-1-1: Nashville, Grey's Anatomy, and R.J. Decker, ABC's lineup of procedurals premiering their new seasons this January all concluded their most recent seasons last spring. Whereas fans of the aforementioned shows only had to wait for the length of the standard summer hiatus, though, fans of the second group of shows will have had to wait up to nine months by the time they return.

For a show like Will Trent, which has been on this timeline since its debut, this is to be expected. The Rookie and High Potential, on the other hand, initially got to air in both the fall and the spring, and have since been relegated to just the latter. For two of ABC's most popular shows, it's already disappointing that they only get to air for a few months of the year. Now, though, there are just under two months until these shows return the first full week of January, and it's frustrating that their return dates have not been announced until last week.

The Rookie has been on the spring release schedule for three seasons now, but High Potential has only just been moved to this lineup. It's a particularly jarring choice for High Potential, considering the series is only on its third season, and the show's second season had monumental records of success. Just as the series was really gaining momentum, it was put on break for nine months, leaving fans to speculate on their own about the fallout of the Season 2 finale's intense cliffhanger ending. Fans of The Rookie, meanwhile, may be used to this by now, but it is still frustrating to watch a beloved Network TV show only air for about a third of the year, then go on break for the rest of it.

The Rookie started as a show about a man starting over at forty-five and turned into a proper ensemble drama somewhere around season three. Here is which of them you are, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

You started late and you are not embarrassed about it. Nolan walks into the academy at forty-five surrounded by people half his age, and the show is honest that this is both his biggest disadvantage and the only reason he is any good at the job.

You are better at this than people expect and you intend to keep proving it. Chen goes from rookie to the best undercover officer in the division, which works because she is genuinely good at becoming somebody else and genuinely bad at pretending she does not care.

You are hard on people because you have decided that is what caring looks like. Bradford is introduced as the worst training officer in the building and slowly revealed as the one who takes the job most seriously, which are the same fact seen from two angles.

You said what you wanted and then you went and got it. Lopez wanted detective from the first episode, said so out loud, and got there by being better at the work than the people who were quieter about wanting it.

There are a lot of benefits to being a fan of a Network TV show, from getting to watch the episodes live alongside other fans to getting to speculate each week about what will happen next. The best part, though, is loving a show with a predictable release schedule. When series then start changing their release schedule to only air for half the time, it is incredibly disappointing to fans. It means potentially fewer episodes for the new season, as well as a much longer wait in between seasons, dampening some of the excitement and anticipation earned by the finales of the previous seasons.

In a perfect world, ABC would move High Potential and The Rookie back to its fall release schedule, but as it stands, the network just needs to do better by the procedurals in its spring lineup. Both of these shows excellently set up suspense ahead of their new seasons by ending their most recent ones with massive cliffhangers after two explosive episodes. For The Rookie, the fan-favorite pairing of Lucy Chen (Melissa O'Neil) and Tim Bradford (Eric Winter) finally got engaged in a beautiful beach proposal, only to both get abducted seconds later. High Potential, on the other hand, introduced another new twist in the ongoing mystery of what happened to Roman Sinquerra. After Captain Nick Wagner (Steve Howey) went to a meetup to get more information on this mystery, Morgan Gillory (Kaitlin Olson) found him shot and left for dead, leaving Wagner's fate up in the air over the hiatus.

When both of these series concluded their most recent seasons, fans were left champing at the bit to find out what happens next. While there are still devoted fans excited for these series to return, there has no doubt been a loss of momentum for both of these series after their unusually long break. Most fans will likely have to do a refresher on the events of the previous seasons to remember the main events ahead of their returns, and while that's become standard for shows on streaming now, this is still atypical of Network TV shows. ABC needs to do better with the shows in its spring lineup, and to stop moving shows to mid-season after they've previously been airing for the entire season.

High Potential returns to ABC on Tuesday, January 5, at 9:00 P.M. EST. The Rookie returns to ABC the following night, on Wednesday, January 6, at 9:00 P.M. EST.

#3482. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3481. 'I've Had It' Host Unfazed As Advertisers Drop Out Amid Charlie Kirk Backlash

Jennifer Welch says her podcast isn't going anywhere ... even as more advertisers head for the exits amid backlash over the hosts laughing at a joke about Charlie Kirk’s assassination.

The “I’ve Had It” cohost tells TMZ ... “We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren't going anywhere," adding ... "Each and every day we will relentlessly fight for equality and justice for every American and we enthusiastically welcome the nearly 40,000 new followers that have come to our channel in the last few days."

Meanwhile, more brands begin to distance themselves, with Jones Road Beauty telling TMZ ... it is no longer a sponsor of the podcast, adding the brand does not condone violence of any kind. A spokesperson for ZipRecruiter tells us "We do not have future ads placed on this show."

An Ethos spokesperson also says ... "We don’t condone or align with the comments made on the “I’ve had it” podcast. What was said on this show doesn’t reflect our values, and we don’t condone violence in any form. We’ve ended our advertising relationship and won’t be working with them moving forward."

Additionally, a spokesperson for Honeylove adds "At Honeylove, we believe violence of any kind is unacceptable. We understand the concerns raised about the recent comments associated with the I’ve Had It podcast and want to be clear that these views do not reflect our values as a brand."

They continue ... "We have ended our advertising partnership with the podcast. We take seriously the responsibility we have as a brand to be thoughtful about the partnerships we support, and we appreciate those who took the time to share their concerns with us."

Tim McDowd, a spokesperson for Ember Mugs, tells TMZ ... "I can confirm the company ended their advertising relationship with the podcast."

The latest confirmations come as the podcast, hosted by Welch and Angie "Pumps" Sullivan, faces mounting backlash after the two laughed at a social media post making light of Kirk's killing.

The controversy erupted after Welch read a post during Thursday's episode saying, "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." Both hosts laughed, sparking outrage and calls for advertisers to pull their support.

The hosts apologized Saturday, acknowledging the joke was insensitive and expressing regret over their reaction. They also announced a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety ... but the apology hasn't stopped the fallout, with several other companies also distancing themselves from the show.

Momentous announced it no longer sponsors or partners with the podcast, saying the hosts' comments do not reflect its values and that the company does not condone violence of any kind. Chewy also confirmed it does not sponsor or support the podcast, condemning violence and saying the hosts' comments do not reflect the company's values.

Other companies, including Cash App and Casper, have also confirmed they're no longer sponsoring the show.

#3479. ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Officially Delivers Record-Breaking Box Office Debut

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. He also writes obsessively about the box office, charting the many hits and misses that are released weekly, and how their commercial performance shapes public perception. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

Two overseas titles secured spots on the top-five list of the domestic box office this weekend, with Godzilla Minus Zero claiming the number-one spot and Ramayana: Rise of a Legend finishing fifth. While the top-five list was bookended by the two international movies, three vastly different homegrown titles took the remaining three spots. Among them were two new releases, the animated offering The Cat in the Hat, and the period musical Drummer Boy.

Ramayana: Rise of a Legend is the most expensive Indian film of all time, with a reported production budget of approximately $200 million. The movie is the first part of a planned duology, with the second installment currently slated for a 2028 release. A grand international publicity tour was mounted to promote the mythological epic, necessitated by its massive production cost. As a rule of thumb, a film this size needs to gross twice its reported budget to break even. Ramayana got off to a lukewarm start, with $55 million globally and around $12 million domestically this past weekend.

Godzilla Minus Zero, on the other hand, had built-in buzz thanks to the positive word-of-mouth earned by its predecessor, Godzilla Minus One. Released in 2023, the previous installment grossed more than $110 million worldwide against a reported budget of $10 million. The movie broke box-office records for international titles in North America, having grossed more than $55 million in its theatrical run. Godzilla Minus One rode a wave of positive buzz to win the Best Visual Effects Oscar, beating out mega-budget behemoths.

The 2023 film was set in post-war Japan, serving as an allegory for the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Many viewed it as a companion piece to Christopher Nolan's biographical thriller Oppenheimer, which was released the same year. Like Nolan's film, Godzilla Minus One was critically acclaimed. It now holds a near-perfect 99% score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Godzilla Minus Zero has also received positive reviews. The film is currently sitting at a "Certified Fresh" 90% critics score and a "Verified Hot" 96% audience score on the aggregator website, where the consensus reads, "Keeping its epic action rooted in human interest, Godzilla Minus Zero solidifies director Takashi Yamazaki's take on the King of Monsters as one of the mightiest yet by upping the ante without losing sight of its lovable characters." Buoyed by positive reviews, the film grossed nearly $32 million in its domestic debut, nearly tripling the $11 million opening-weekend haul of its predecessor.

This is also the biggest debut for an international live-action movie. Godzilla Minus Zero's global opening stood at $63 million against a reported budget of $15 million. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.
